title: The Fire Beneath the Kettle
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 30 of 40
content:
The campfire was small enough that I could have stepped over it.

Iroh sat before it as though he were looking into a room full of people. The kettle hung from a short iron hook. Rain had stopped an hour earlier, and the wood was damp around the edges.

"You've been staring at that flame for ten minutes," I said.

"Only eight."

"You counted?"

"I was hoping you would notice."

I sat on the dry side of the blanket. We'd spent the day following the upper river road toward Ba Sing Se, carrying our packs and arguing about the best place to buy breakfast. The town we'd stayed in was behind us. Ahead, the road bent along a stand of trees to a small travelers' shelter where we intended to spend the night.

I had asked whether he would show me firebending as something other than a weapon.

It sounded romantic when I said it.

It became much less romantic when I realized I knew almost nothing about fire safety.

"Before we begin," he said, "what would you like to learn?"

"Why you treat a cooking fire as though it has opinions."

He laughed.

"An excellent question."

"Also how you can warm tea without setting everything on fire."

"Another excellent question. I suspect this one will be more practical."

He began with the ordinary work. We cleared the wet leaves from around the stones. He tested the kettle hook. I brought water from the stream and filtered it through the camp cloth as he'd shown me earlier in the trip. Neither of us treated bending as a substitute for making sure the pot could stand safely.

Then he held his hands near the flame.

"Fire is easy to fear when all you have seen is what it can destroy," he said. "But look at what we ask this one to do."

"Boil water."

"Yes. Warm two travelers. Dry a pair of very unhappy socks."

"They're your socks."

"Then their unhappiness is particularly severe."

I laughed.

He breathed in slowly, then let a thin ribbon of fire brighten in the hearth without climbing beyond the stones. He did not strike a heroic pose. He moved with the care of someone whose body had learned both force and restraint.

I felt the warmth rise against my face.

"That isn't a trick," I said.

"No. And it isn't a command to the fire to obey a more important man. It is something I practice with respect."

I watched the flames settle.

"Can someone learn that without bending?"

"You can learn to tend a flame, understand its fuel and air, recognize when it has become unsafe. Bending is one way of working with fire, not the only way of caring for it."

I liked that answer.

A traveler with a cart arrived while the kettle warmed. She had been delayed by a washed-out patch of road and asked whether the shelter had room for another bedroll. Iroh stood and offered her space beside the far wall.

She looked at the fire.

"Will it stay small?"

"Yes," he answered. "And if you would prefer it out while you sleep, tell us."

The traveler thanked him and settled her bag.

I expected him to keep talking about firebending. Instead he helped her find a dry place for her boots and asked whether she had enough water. She did. She asked for nothing more.

When he sat beside me again, I said, "You didn't perform for her."

"She wanted shelter, not a demonstration."

"That may be the most important part of your lesson."

He smiled.

The kettle began to hum.

Iroh lifted it from the hook and let the fire ease back to ordinary embers. We poured tea into two cups. He tasted his and looked pleased.

"Would you like to know what I once believed?" he asked.

I nodded, but I didn't move closer until he made room.

"When I was young, I was praised for power that frightened people. It is possible to become very good at something before you ask whether you should be proud of the way you use it."

I looked toward the dark trees.

"Do you miss being powerful?"

He was quiet for a long moment.

"I have not stopped being powerful," he said. "I have stopped treating every situation as an invitation to demonstrate it."

The distinction made me look at him differently.

He still carried the old general's posture. He still noticed where every traveler sat, how quickly somebody reached for a bag, whether a door could be closed from the inside. Those habits might protect people or make them feel watched, depending on what he did with them.

"Do you want me to tell you when that posture makes me nervous?" I asked.

"Please."

"I did get nervous when you checked all the exits in the inn yesterday."

He closed his eyes.

"I am sorry. I was worried about the rain and made no explanation."

"You don't have to explain every thought. But I'd rather you tell me you're checking the roof than let me imagine you're waiting for an attack."

He opened his eyes.

"That is a fair request."

The traveler at the far end of the shelter had begun to snore, very gently.

I tried not to laugh.

Iroh heard it, glanced toward her, and smiled.

"This is what I wished to learn," he said.

"How to ignore snoring?"

"How to be in a place without needing to decide its fate."

I held my cup between my hands. We had discussed my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory before making romance part of our journey. Iroh didn't need to become my sole refuge. Nor did I need to be the person who repaired everything his past had broken.

"Can I ask you one more question?" I said.

"Of course."

"If I tell you I love spending time with you, will you hear it as a request to become someone different?"

"No."

"Good."

He looked at me.

"And if I tell you I value this moment very much, will you hear it as a demand that you never travel elsewhere?"

"No."

He offered his hand.

I took it.

The kettle had cooled. The fire was low, but the stones still held warmth. I moved closer and kissed his cheek, then paused.

"May I?"

His smile was soft.

"Please."

We kissed slowly beneath the shelter roof. Somewhere beyond the trees, water moved over the river stones. The traveler slept on, uninterested in our private lives.

Later we banked the embers and checked that the fire was safe. Iroh put the kettle away; I hung his unhappy socks where they might dry by morning.

Before sleep, I wrote a line in my notebook.

*Power was not the part I loved. It was the care he chose when nobody was asking him to win.*

In the morning, the socks were still damp.

Iroh declared this a grave injustice.

We laughed over breakfast, packed the kettle, and continued toward the city without lighting any heroic flames.

bridge_outro: The shop kettle had hardly stopped steaming when a small brass bell rang from Jasmine Steps. Iroh and I crossed into the Lanternweald to find Severus standing beside the community garden, frowning at a plant label. 'This is not mountain mint,' he informed Iroh. 'It has been mislabeled.' I waited for offense. Instead Iroh looked closely at the leaves and asked for a lesson. By sunset, the two had produced a precise growing chart, an excellent pot of tea, and only one argument about whether measurements were a substitute for good judgment. Seeing Iroh learn without pretending to know everything made me love him in another, quieter way.
